tf.statement: A real \(m\times n\) matrix represents a linear map from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R^m\).
tf.explanation: Its n columns multiply the n input coordinates, producing m output coordinates.

tf.statement: If both \(AB\) and \(BA\) are defined and have the same shape, they must be equal.
tf.explanation: Equal shape does not imply equality. For example, \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) give \(AB=B\) but \(BA=0\).

tf.statement: The correct transpose rule for a product is \((AB)^T=A^TB^T\).
tf.explanation: The order reverses: \((AB)^T=B^TA^T\). The stated right side can even have incompatible dimensions.

tf.statement: If \(A\in\mathbb R^{2\times4}\) has full rank, then \(Ax=0\) has only the zero solution.
tf.explanation: Full rank here means rank 2, not full column rank 4. Rank-nullity gives a two-dimensional nullspace.
tf.source: PDF p.8; supplementary consequence from PDF pp.4,8

tf.statement: A square matrix has an inverse if and only if its determinant is nonzero.
tf.explanation: A zero determinant characterizes singularity; the cofactor inverse is defined when the determinant is nonzero.

tf.statement: If two real vectors have zero inner product, at least one of them must be the zero vector.
tf.explanation: Nonzero perpendicular vectors, such as the two coordinate vectors in the plane, have zero inner product.

tf.statement: For \(x,y\in\mathbb R^3\), the outer product \(xy^T\) is a scalar.
tf.explanation: The outer product is \(3\times3\); the inner product \(x^Ty\) is a scalar.

tf.statement: Every real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix is invertible.
tf.explanation: The zero matrix and a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries 1 and 0 are positive semidefinite but singular.

tf.statement: Every invertible real symmetric matrix has only positive eigenvalues.
tf.explanation: Invertibility excludes zero eigenvalues but allows negative ones; for example, the diagonal matrix with entries 1 and -1 is invertible and indefinite.

tf.statement: Every pair of eigenvectors of a real symmetric matrix is automatically orthogonal, including pairs with the same eigenvalue.
tf.explanation: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal. Within a repeated eigenspace, vectors may be nonorthogonal, although an orthonormal basis can be chosen; the identity matrix is a counterexample to the unconditional claim.
tf.source: PDF p.15; clarification of repeated eigenvalues

tf.statement: Under the lecture convention, the gradient of a scalar function of \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is an \(n\times1\) column vector.
tf.explanation: The listed partial derivatives are transposed into a column.

tf.statement: If \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(x\), then its Hessian at \(x\) is symmetric.
tf.explanation: Continuity of the second partial derivatives ensures equality of mixed partial derivatives. The regularity condition makes the symmetry statement precise.

mc.stem: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\-1&0&3\end{pmatrix}\), with columns \(a_1,a_2,a_3\), and \(x=(2,-1,1)^T\). Select every correct statement.

options.why: The first row gives 2-2=0; the second gives -2+3=1.
Matrix-vector multiplication weights the columns by the coordinates of x.
A transpose is 3 by 2 and requires a two-dimensional input.

options.text: Every vector \(Ax\), as \(x\) varies, lies in the span of the columns of \(A\).
options.why: The column expansion proves membership in that span.

mc.stem: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\). Select every correct trace identity.

options.why: Both equal \(\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}b_{ji}\), even when the square products have different sizes.
The diagonal entry indexed by j is the squared Euclidean norm of column j.
For two 2 by 2 identity matrices the left side is 2 and the right side is 4.
Transposition leaves every diagonal entry unchanged.

mc.stem: Let \(A,B\) be invertible real square matrices of the same size. Select every valid formula.

options.why: The general inverse rule reverses the order. The stated expression works under additional commutation conditions, not in general.
Transpose the identities defining the inverse.
The correct scalar factor is one half.
The determinant is multiplicative for square matrices, rather than additive across a product.

mc.stem: For \(x=(-2,1,2)^T\), select every correct norm value.

options.why: The sum of absolute entries is 2+1+2.
The sum of squared entries is 4+1+4=9.
The largest absolute entry is 2; 3 is the Euclidean norm in this example.
Absolute values must be applied to individual coordinates before summation.

mc.stem: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) satisfy \(Q^TQ=I\). Select every statement that holds for all real \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\).

options.why: Insert Q transpose Q between x transpose and y.
The squared distance is preserved by the same inner-product identity.
A rotation can turn (1,0) into (1/sqrt(2),1/sqrt(2)), changing its 1-norm.

options.text: If x and y are nonzero, their angle is preserved by Q.
options.why: The inner product and both Euclidean lengths are preserved, so the cosine of the angle is preserved.

mc.stem: Let \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\) both be nonzero. Select every correct statement about outer products.

options.why: Every column is a multiple of x and at least one column is nonzero.
Its transpose is itself, and \(z^Txx^Tz=(x^Tz)^2\geq0\).
Sum the diagonal entries \(x_i y_i\).
For distinct coordinate vectors these matrices have their single nonzero entry in different positions.

mc.stem: A Cholesky factorization is given as \(C=T^TT\), where \(T\) is a nonsingular upper triangular real matrix. Select every correct conclusion.

options.why: For nonzero \(z\), \(z^TCz=\|Tz\|_2^2>0\).
The product of the diagonal entries is \(\det T\); \(\det C\) is its square. For \(T=2I_2\), the two claimed quantities are 16 and 4.

options.text: The diagonal entry \(c_{ii}\) always equals the squared length of row \(i\) of \(T\).
options.why: In \(T^TT\), \(c_{ii}\) is the squared length of column \(i\) of \(T\). Row lengths instead form the diagonal of \(TT^T\).

options.text: The same factor always also satisfies \(C=TT^T\).
options.why: For T with rows (1,1) and (0,1), T transpose T differs from T T transpose.

mc.source: PDF pp.7,13; supplementary determinant and column consequences

mc.stem: Consider a proposed eigendecomposition \(A=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}\), with diagonal \(\Lambda\). Select every correct statement.

options.text: The columns of Q must be linearly independent.
options.why: The inverse of Q exists only when its columns form a basis.

options.text: Normalizing every column of Q to length one is sufficient to replace the inverse by its transpose.
options.why: Unit lengths do not ensure mutual orthogonality.

options.text: A real symmetric matrix permits an orthogonal choice of Q and real diagonal entries in the decomposition.
options.why: The spectral theorem supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis.

options.text: Every real square matrix has such a decomposition with a real invertible Q and a real diagonal Lambda.
options.why: A real matrix can have nonreal eigenvalues or fail to have enough independent eigenvectors.

mc.stem: Let \(A,B\) be real symmetric PSD matrices of the same size. Select every statement that always holds.

options.why: Its quadratic form is the sum of two nonnegative quadratic forms.
The transpose of AB is BA, and PSD matrices need not commute.
Take \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\), \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\), and \(x=(1,-1)^T\). Both matrices are PSD, but the quadratic value is -1.

options.text: For every real matrix \(R\) with compatible dimensions, \(R^TAR\) is PSD.
options.why: It is symmetric and \(z^TR^TARz=(Rz)^TA(Rz)\geq0\).

mc.stem: For fixed \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), let \(f(u,v)=u^TAv\), with \(u\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(v\in\mathbb R^n\). Select every correct statement.

options.why: The coefficient of the differential du is Av.
Write the scalar as v transpose A transpose u and differentiate.

options.text: When \(v\) is fixed, the Hessian with respect to \(u\) is the zero \(m\times m\) matrix.
options.why: The function is linear in u, so its gradient does not depend on u.

options.text: When \(u\) is fixed, \(\nabla_v f=Au\) regardless of dimensions.
options.why: The transpose is required, and Au may not even be defined.

mc.stem: Let \(C\) be a real symmetric positive definite matrix and \(g(C)=\log\det C\). Matrix gradients use \(dg=\operatorname{tr}((\nabla_Cg)^T\,dC)\). Select every correct statement.

options.why: The general inverse-transpose expression equals the inverse for symmetric C.

options.text: For a symmetric perturbation \(H\), the directional derivative is \(\operatorname{tr}(C^{-1}H)\).
options.why: Substitute H for dC in the differential.

options.text: The real logarithm of the determinant is defined for every invertible real matrix.
options.why: An invertible matrix can have a negative determinant, whose real logarithm is undefined.

options.text: For positive scalar \(c\), if \(C=cI_n\), then \(g(C)=n\log c\).
options.why: The determinant is c to the nth power.
The partial derivatives are \(2x_1x_2\) and \(x_1^2+6x_2\).
Its quadratic form is 2(a+b) squared plus 4 b squared, positive away from zero.
Its determinant is -4; directly its form is positive at (0,1) and negative at (2,-1).

options.text: The Hessian is constant because f is a polynomial.
options.why: The general Hessian has entries \(2x_2,2x_1,2x_1,6\), so it depends on \(x\).

long.title: The nullspace and definiteness of a Gram matrix

parts.question: For any real \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), prove \(\operatorname{null}(A^TA)=\operatorname{null}(A)\). Your proof must establish both inclusions without assuming \(A\) is square.
parts.solution: If \(Ax=0\), then \(A^TAx=A^T0=0\), proving one inclusion. Conversely, if \(A^TAx=0\), left-multiply by \(x^T\) to get \[0=x^TA^TAx=(Ax)^T(Ax)=\|Ax\|_2^2.\] A sum of squares is zero only when every coordinate vanishes, so \(Ax=0\). This gives the other inclusion for any rectangular shape. Award one mark for the first inclusion and two for the norm argument in the second.

parts.question: Use the result to prove that \(A^TA\) is PSD, that its rank equals the rank of \(A\), and that it is PD if and only if \(A\) has full column rank. Explain the case \(m<n\).
parts.solution: The matrix is symmetric because \((A^TA)^T=A^TA\), and \(x^TA^TAx=\|Ax\|_2^2\geq0\), so it is PSD. Both maps have domain \(\mathbb R^n\) and the same nullspace. Rank-nullity therefore gives \(\operatorname{rank}(A^TA)=n-\dim\operatorname{null}(A)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\). Its quadratic form is strictly positive for every nonzero x exactly when \(Ax=0\) has no nonzero solution, equivalently rank A=n. If m<n, rank A is at most m<n; hence the Gram matrix is necessarily singular and cannot be PD, even if A has full rank in the rectangular sense. Award one mark each for PSD, rank equality, the PD equivalence, and the wide-matrix case.

parts.question: For \(\mu>0\), prove \(A^TA+\mu I_n\) is PD for every \(A\). Give a lower bound on its quadratic form and explain why its inverse exists.
parts.solution: For every nonzero x, \[x^T(A^TA+\mu I_n)x=\|Ax\|_2^2+\mu\|x\|_2^2\geq\mu\|x\|_2^2>0.\] The matrix is symmetric, so it is PD. If it had a nonzero null vector, its quadratic form there would be zero, contradicting this bound. Thus its nullspace is trivial and, being square, it is invertible. Award one mark for the expansion, one for the strict bound, and one for invertibility.

long.title: Differentiate a nonsymmetric quadratic and a bilinear form

parts.question: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be fixed, with no symmetry assumption, and \(f(x)=x^TAx\). Expand \(f(x+h)-f(x)\) and derive its gradient and Hessian. Explain precisely why the formula \(2Ax\) need not be correct.
parts.solution: The exact expansion is \[f(x+h)-f(x)=h^TAx+x^TAh+h^TAh=((A+A^T)x)^Th+h^TAh.\] The last term is quadratic in h and is the higher-order remainder. Thus \(df=((A+A^T)x)^Tdx\), giving \(\nabla f=(A+A^T)x\) and \(\nabla^2 f=A+A^T\). The expression 2Ax agrees for all x if and only if A is symmetric; otherwise one must account for both appearances of x in the quadratic. Award one mark for expansion, one for identifying the linear differential, and one each for the gradient and Hessian with the symmetry qualification.

parts.question: Decompose \(A=S+K\), where \(S=(A+A^T)/2\) and \(K=(A-A^T)/2\). Prove \(x^TKx=0\), and show that knowledge of \(x^TAx\) for every real \(x\) cannot identify \(K\).
parts.solution: K is skew-symmetric. The scalar \(s=x^TKx\) equals its transpose, which is \(x^TK^Tx=-x^TKx=-s\); hence s=0 over the real numbers. Therefore \(x^TAx=x^TSx\) for all x. Adding any skew-symmetric matrix to A changes K but leaves every quadratic-form value unchanged, so those values cannot identify K. Award one mark for skew symmetry, one for the scalar-transpose proof, and one for the identification conclusion.

parts.question: For fixed \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), derive the first differential of \(g(u,v)=u^TBv\) and both partial gradients. Then state the derivative along differentiable paths \(u(t),v(t)\).
parts.solution: Expanding the perturbed bilinear form gives \[dg=(du)^TBv+u^TB(dv)=(Bv)^Tdu+(B^Tu)^Tdv.\] The product \((du)^TB(dv)\) is second order and does not enter the first differential. Thus \(\nabla_u g=Bv\) and \(\nabla_v g=B^Tu\). Along paths, both arguments vary and the chain rule gives \[\frac{d}{dt}g(u(t),v(t))=u'(t)^TBv(t)+u(t)^TBv'(t).\] Award one mark for the differential, one for both gradients, and one for the two-term path derivative.

parts.question: Let \(A=A^T\), \(Au=\alpha u\), and \(Av=\beta v\), with nonzero eigenvectors and \(\alpha\neq\beta\). Prove \(u^Tv=0\). Explain what must be changed when the eigenvalues are equal.
parts.solution: Symmetry yields \[\alpha u^Tv=(Au)^Tv=u^TA^Tv=u^TAv=\beta u^Tv.\] Hence \((\alpha-\beta)u^Tv=0\), and distinct eigenvalues imply orthogonality. When the eigenvalues coincide, this equation imposes no orthogonality condition; for A=I any nonzero vector is an eigenvector. One can choose an orthonormal basis within each repeated eigenspace, producing the orthogonal Q in the spectral theorem. Award two marks for the equality and conclusion, and one for the repeated-eigenvalue qualification.

parts.question: Using the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices, prove that \(A\) is PSD if and only if all its eigenvalues are nonnegative, and PD if and only if all are positive. Also establish the relation between rank and nonzero eigenvalues.
parts.solution: Write \(A=Q\Lambda Q^T\) with Q orthogonal, and put \(z=Q^Tx\). Then \[x^TAx=z^T\Lambda z=\sum_i\lambda_i z_i^2.\] If all eigenvalues are nonnegative this is nonnegative, proving PSD; if all are positive and x is nonzero then z is nonzero, so the sum is strictly positive, proving PD. Conversely, using a unit eigenvector \(q_i\) gives \(q_i^TAq_i=\lambda_i\), forcing nonnegative or strictly positive eigenvalues under PSD or PD respectively. Multiplication by invertible Q and Q transpose preserves rank, so rank A=rank Lambda, the number of nonzero diagonal eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. Award one mark for the diagonal quadratic form, one for sufficiency, one for necessity, and one for rank.

parts.question: For nonzero \(x\), derive the Rayleigh quotient bounds \(\lambda_{\min}\leq x^TAx/(x^Tx)\leq\lambda_{\max}\). Characterize equality at each endpoint.
parts.solution: Orthogonality gives \(x^Tx=z^Tz\), so \[\frac{x^TAx}{x^Tx}=\sum_i\lambda_i\frac{z_i^2}{\sum_j z_j^2}.\] The weights are nonnegative and sum to one, making this a weighted average of the eigenvalues and proving the bounds. Equality with the smallest eigenvalue holds exactly when all nonzero z coordinates belong to that eigenspace; equivalently x lies in the minimum-eigenvalue eigenspace. The analogous statement holds at the maximum. These conditions also cover repeated extremes and scalar multiples of the identity. Award one mark for the weighted average, one for the bounds, and one for the endpoint characterization.

long.title: Build an orthogonal projector from an orthonormal basis

parts.question: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}\) have orthonormal columns, with \(1\leq r\leq m\). Define \(P=QQ^T\). Prove \(P^T=P\), \(P^2=P\), and \(Pz=z\) for every \(z\in\operatorname{col}(Q)\).
parts.solution: Transposition gives \(P^T=(QQ^T)^T=QQ^T=P\). Orthonormality means \(Q^TQ=I_r\), so \(P^2=Q(Q^TQ)Q^T=QQ^T=P\). If \(z=Qc\), then \(Pz=QQ^TQc=Qc=z\). Each identity follows from the stated shapes and does not require the rectangular Q to have a two-sided inverse. Award one mark for each identity.

parts.question: For an arbitrary \(y\in\mathbb R^m\), show that \(y=Py+(I-P)y\) is a decomposition into a vector in \(\operatorname{col}(Q)\) and a vector orthogonal to that space. Derive a Pythagorean norm identity.
parts.solution: The sum equals y by direct cancellation, and \(Py=Q(Q^Ty)\) is in the column space. Let \(r_y=(I-P)y\). Then \[Q^Tr_y=Q^Ty-Q^TQQ^Ty=0,\] so the residual is orthogonal to every vector Qc in the space, including Py. Expanding the squared norm and using the zero cross term yields \[\|y\|_2^2=\|Py\|_2^2+\|(I-P)y\|_2^2.\] Award one mark each for the sum/membership, residual orthogonality, the zero cross term, and the norm identity.

parts.question: Prove that \(Py\) is the unique nearest vector to \(y\) in \(\operatorname{col}(Q)\). Then prove \(\|Py\|_2\leq\|y\|_2\) and give its equality condition.
parts.solution: For any z in the column space, write \(y-z=(I-P)y+(Py-z)\). The summands are orthogonal, hence \[\|y-z\|_2^2=\|(I-P)y\|_2^2+\|Py-z\|_2^2.\] The minimum is attained exactly at z=Py, so the nearest vector is unique. The Pythagorean identity from the previous part gives \(\|Py\|_2\leq\|y\|_2\), with equality exactly when \((I-P)y=0\), equivalently y lies in the column space. Award one mark for the distance identity, one for uniqueness, and one for the norm bound and equality condition.

long.title: A rectangular sensor map: rank, Cholesky, and residual geometry

parts.question: A sensor model is \(Az\), where \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), and the observed vector is \(b=(2,0,1)^T\). Compute \(G=A^TA\) and \(A^Tb\), establish the column rank of \(A\), and decide whether \(G\) is PD.
parts.solution: Direct multiplication gives \[G=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad A^Tb=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}.\] The two columns (1,1,0) and (0,1,1) are independent: their first and third coordinates force both coefficients of a zero linear combination to vanish. Thus rank A=2, its full column rank. G is PD by the Gram result; directly its quadratic form is \((z_1+z_2)^2+z_1^2+z_2^2>0\) for nonzero z. Award one mark for both products, one for column independence, and one for PD.

parts.question: Find an upper triangular \(T\) with positive diagonal such that \(G=T^TT\), and verify the product.
parts.solution: Write \(T=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\0&d\end{pmatrix}\). Matching entries requires \(a^2=2\), \(ac=1\), and \(c^2+d^2=2\). Positive diagonal entries give \[T=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt2&1/\sqrt2\\0&\sqrt{3/2}\end{pmatrix}.\] The resulting product has entries 2,1,1, and \(1/2+3/2=2\), matching G. Award one mark for the matching equations, one for T, and one for verification.

parts.question: Find \(z_*\) by solving \(Gz_*=A^Tb\). Compute \(r=b-Az_*\), verify \(A^Tr=0\), and use a squared-distance expansion to show that this solution gives the unique best least-squares fit.
parts.solution: The equations are \(2z_1+z_2=2\) and \(z_1+2z_2=1\), yielding \(z_*=(1,0)^T\). Its fitted vector is \((1,1,0)^T\), and \(r=(1,-1,1)^T\). Then \(A^Tr=(1-1,-1+1)^T=0\). For any perturbation d, \[\|b-A(z_*+d)\|_2^2=\|r-Ad\|_2^2=3+\|Ad\|_2^2,\] because the cross term vanishes. Full column rank means \(Ad=0\) only when d=0, establishing the unique minimizer and minimum squared error 3. Award one mark each for z, residual/orthogonality, the expansion, and uniqueness.

parts.question: Find the eigenvalues of \(G\) and an orthonormal eigenbasis. Express \(\|Ad\|_2^2\) using the coordinates of \(d\) in that basis.
parts.solution: The normalized vectors \(q_+=(1,1)^T/\sqrt2\) and \(q_-=(1,-1)^T/\sqrt2\) have eigenvalues 3 and 1. If \(d=\alpha q_++\beta q_-\), then \(\|Ad\|_2^2=d^TGd=3\alpha^2+\beta^2\). Thus equal-sized coefficient changes along the first direction create three times the squared sensor-output change. Award one mark for the eigenpairs and one for the expression.

long.title: A nonsymmetric representation of a quadratic objective

parts.question: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^TBx-c^Tx\), where \(B=\begin{pmatrix}4&5\\-1&6\end{pmatrix}\), \(c=(6,8)^T\), and \(x\in\mathbb R^2\). Compute its gradient and Hessian. Identify the symmetric matrix governing its quadratic part.
parts.solution: Its symmetric part is \[S=(B+B^T)/2=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&6\end{pmatrix}.\] Because the skew part contributes zero to a quadratic form, \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^TSx-c^Tx\). Differentiating gives \(\nabla f(x)=Sx-c\) and \(\nabla^2f(x)=S\). Using Bx-c would be incorrect because B is not symmetric. Award one mark each for S, the gradient, and the Hessian.

parts.question: Find the eigenvalues of the Hessian and decide whether it is PD, PSD but not PD, or indefinite. Give a quadratic-form verification of strict positivity as an independent check.
parts.solution: The characteristic polynomial is \[(4-\lambda)(6-\lambda)-4=\lambda^2-10\lambda+20,\] with roots \(5-\sqrt5\) and \(5+\sqrt5\), both positive. The Hessian is PD. Independently, for \(u=(u_1,u_2)^T\), \[u^TSu=4u_1^2+4u_1u_2+6u_2^2=4(u_1+u_2/2)^2+5u_2^2,\] which is strictly positive for every nonzero u. Award one mark for the eigenvalues, one for the classification, and one for the completed-square check.

parts.question: Solve for the stationary point, compute its objective value, and prove that it is the unique global minimizer.
parts.solution: Solving \(Sx=c\) gives \(4x_1+2x_2=6\) and \(2x_1+6x_2=8\), hence \(x_*=(1,1)^T\). Its value is \(f(x_*)=7-14=-7\). Using \(Sx_*=c\), an exact expansion gives \[f(x)-f(x_*)=\tfrac12(x-x_*)^TS(x-x_*).\] Positive definiteness makes this quantity positive for every \(x\ne x_*\), proving the unique global minimum. Award one mark for the point, one for its value, and one for the expansion and uniqueness.

parts.question: Start at \(x_0=0\) and take one gradient step \(x_1=x_0-\eta\nabla f(x_0)\), with \(\eta>0\). Find the complete range of step sizes that strictly decreases the objective on this first step. Also find the best step size along this direction.
parts.solution: At zero the gradient is -c, so \(x_1=\eta c=(6\eta,8\eta)^T\). Since \(c^Tc=100\) and \(c^TSc=720\), \[f(x_1)=360\eta^2-100\eta.\] As f(0)=0, strict decrease holds exactly when \(0<\eta<100/360=5/18\). Differentiating this scalar quadratic gives the best step \(\eta=100/720=5/36\), giving \(x_1=(5/6,10/9)^T\) and value \(-125/18\). This is a one-step calculation along the specified direction. Award one mark for the quadratic expression, one for the strict interval, and one for the optimal step.
